1882: Vaccine Act procedure: the Court of Federal Claims' statutory authority to set aside the special master's findings of fact and conclusions of law that are arbitrary, capricious or not in accordance with law.

Where, as here, a special master misapprehends a petitioner's theory of causation, misconstrues his medical records, and makes factual inferences wholly unsupported by the record, the Court of Federal Claims is not only authorized, but obliged, to set aside the special master's findings of fact and conclusions of law.
2824: Vaccine Act procedure: dismissal of vaccine petition for failure to prosecute was not an abuse of discretion
we find there was no abuse of discretion in dismissing the Appellants' petition for failure to prosecute.
2831: Vaccine Act procedure: remand ordered to a different special master because the original Special Master repeatedly adhered to an erroneous view after instructions to the contrary.
we believe that fundamental fairness is best served by assigning the case to a different special master on remand.
3716: Vaccine Act procedure: whether the special master could decide the case on written submissions without an evidentiary hearing; upheld.
the Vaccine Rules explicitly authorize a Special Master to "decide a case on the basis of written submissions without conducting an evidentiary hearing."
3757: Vaccine Act non-causation requirement: whether Wyatt proved her off-Table injury lasted at least six months under 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-11(c)(1)(D)(i). Court held the finding was not arbitrary and capricious, so the requirement was not met.
the Special Master correctly found that Wyatt failed to prove her injury lasted at least six months because no medical evidence established Wyatt's continuing injury after January 2013.
3758: Identifiable injury: the Special Master's finding that Wyatt failed to prove any identifiable injury was arbitrary and capricious as to polyarthritis, which the treating physician diagnosed, but the finding on GBS was upheld because the expert opinion was unreliable.
we find, contrary to the Special Master's findings, that Wyatt provided sufficient evidence to prove that she suffered from polyarthritis after receiving the vaccine.
3927: Vaccine Act procedure: whether the special master abused his discretion by ruling on the record over petitioners' objection, without an evidentiary hearing and without their consent.
We conclude that the Special Master did not abuse his discretion by resolving this case on the record.
4003: Vaccine Act procedure: the special master's summary dismissal for failure to prosecute and insufficient evidence, reversed as an abuse of discretion; not a causation ruling.
Summary dismissal of a Vaccine Act case for failure to prosecute in routine cases runs counter to the core purposes of the Vaccine Act.
4086: Vaccine Act eligibility: whether a child in utero when the mother was vaccinated is a 'person' under 42 U.S.C. 300aa-11(c)(1)(B)(i)(III) and 1 U.S.C. 8, so as to have prior presence in the United States.
We hold that 1 U.S.C. § 8's definition of "person" applies to that term as it is used in the Vaccine Act.
4087: Vaccine Act eligibility: whether a six-month entry for medical treatment after vaccination is a 'return to the United States' under 42 U.S.C. 300aa-11(c)(1)(B)(i)(III), requiring some prior residence and intent to resume residence.

We hold that because A.R. D-C.'s entry into the United States to receive medical treatment does not fall within the more narrowly construed meaning of "returned to the United States" that the Vaccine Act's broader context demands, Appellants have not satisfied the requirements of 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-11(c)(1)(B)(i)(III).
4457: Vaccine Act procedure: whether the Special Master abused his discretion by deciding the case without an evidentiary hearing. Court held the hearing decision was committed to the Special Master's discretion and no abuse occurred.
D'Tiole has simply failed to show any abuse of discretion in this determination.
4974: Vaccine Act procedure: dismissal of the petition for failure to prosecute and failure to comply with orders was not an abuse of discretion.
the chief special master did not abuse her discretion in dismissing Mr. Byrd's petition for failure to prosecute.
5203: Vaccine Act non-causation procedural issue: whether the Chief Special Master improperly applied estoppel to deny a fair hearing; the court held she did not.
one reference to other cases rejecting similar claims does not constitute the application of estoppel.
5217: Vaccine Act reasonable-basis standard for fees: the court held the totality-of-the-circumstances objective inquiry survives Simmons and that failing to consider objective evidence is an abuse of discretion.
We see no reasoned basis for abandoning the Claims Court’s objective, totality of the circumstances inquiry.
6552: Vaccine Act timeliness: the central 2002 MMR claim was barred by the Vaccine Act's 36-month statute of limitations, and equitable tolling was not shown; judgment affirmed.
The central claim in Ms. Gaiter's case is the 2002 claim and that claim is barred by the statute of limitations.
6593: Vaccine Act burden of proof: whether the burden shifts to the government in the absence of evidence of causation; majority rejects reversal of burden.
And, finally, contrary to the dissent, it is not the law that, in the absence of evidence of causation, the burden of proof is reversed.
7507: Vaccine Act non-causation issue: whether the special master's finding that Kirby's vaccine injury lasted more than six months (42 U.S.C. 300aa-11(c)(1)(D)) was arbitrary and capricious, including rejection of the Robi presumption that medical records are accurate and complete.
It was not arbitrary and capricious for the special master to find that Ms. Kirby's vaccine injury lasted more than six months.
8308: Vaccine Act timeliness: the Claims Court's post-judgment motion, construed as a Rule 59 motion, was timely filed within 28 days of judgment, so it could toll the appeal period.
So construed, Ling's motion, filed within 28 days of the September 17, 2021 entry of judgment was timely.
8309: Vaccine Act timeliness: Ling's petition for review in the Federal Circuit was untimely under the 60-day limit of 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-12(f), because later reconsideration motions did not toll the appeal period.
his petition for review in this court, filed on August 15, 2022—more than five months after March 3, 2022—clearly did not meet the 60-day time limit of § 300aa-12(f).
9343: Vaccine Act severity requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-11(c)(1)(D): whether B.W.'s later platelet-count testing and bruising constituted 'residual effects' of his vaccine injury lasting more than six months. The court held the testing was not a residual effect because a residual effect must be a change within the patient caused by the vaccine injury, so the petitioner's claim failed the non-causation severity requirement.
We disagree. A residual effect must be a change within the patient that is caused by the vaccine injury.
9399: Vaccine Act procedure: whether the special master erred by not holding a status conference after the government's supplemental Vaccine Rule 4(c) report; the court found no prejudice and did not decide whether Rule 5(a) requires such a conference.
We further conclude that the special master's failure to conduct a status conference after the government submitted its supplemental Vaccine Rule 4(c) report did not prejudice Mr. Webb's claim.
10271: Vaccine Act timeliness: 28 U.S.C. § 2501 six-year statute of limitations and its three-year legal-disability tolling provision held inapplicable, so the 36-month Vaccine Act limitations period governs and the petition was untimely.
We conclude, however, that neither § 2501's statute of limitations nor its tolling provision applies to Vaccine Act petitions.
10272: Equitable tolling based on the minor's mental incapacity rejected: no extraordinary circumstance because the parents, as legal guardians, could have timely filed.

Therefore, we agree with the Court of Federal Claims and the special master that Parents failed to plead facts establishing that W.J.'s mental incapacitation constituted extraordinary circumstances warranting equitable tolling.
10273: Equitable tolling based on minority rejected: the Vaccine Act contains no minority tolling provision.
we conclude that the lack of any statutory provision providing for minority tolling is conclusive proof that Congress did not intend to provide for such tolling.
10274: Equitable tolling based on fraudulent concealment rejected: the information was available in the relevant period, and no intentional concealment was pleaded.
For these reasons, fraudulent concealment cannot serve as a basis for equitable tolling in this case.
10461: Vaccine Act procedure: Greene's jury-trial claim rejected because entitlement claims are heard by special masters and the Seventh Amendment does not apply.
But the Vaccine Act does not authorize juries to hear entitlement claims.
12282: Vaccine Act timeliness: whether equitable tolling applies to the Vaccine Act statute of limitations; court held reasonable diligence was established, reversing the special master and Court of Federal Claims
Accordingly, we reverse the finding that Mr. Chitlik was not reasonably diligent in pursuing his claim.
12283: Vaccine Act timeliness: whether an extraordinary circumstance (USPS delay) supports equitable tolling; court vacated the no-extraordinary-circumstance finding and remanded for case-by-case analysis
We further vacate the special master's finding of no extraordinary circumstances and remand for further proceedings on that issue.
12338: Vaccine Act timeliness: the petition was filed 119 days after the 24-month deadline, and the court held equitable tolling did not make it timely, so the dismissal as time barred was affirmed.
we nonetheless agree with the Court of Federal Claims that Petitioner has not established circumstances warranting equitable tolling for the required 119 days to make the petition timely.
13601: Vaccine Act timeliness: Court of Federal Claims dismissed petitioner's motion for review of the special master's decision as untimely under the 30-day deadline of 42 U.S.C. 300aa-12(e); equitable tolling denied based on claimed mental and physical impairments.
Thus, the Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed Ms. Doe's motion for review because it was not timely filed within the thirty-day deadline.
14154: Vaccine Act severity requirement: construction of 'surgical intervention' under 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-11(c)(1)(D)(iii); court held a diagnostic bone marrow aspiration and biopsy qualifies, reversing the CFC and finding the statutory requirement satisfied for petitioners.

we hold that any surgical procedure—i.e., a surgical act or measure for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes taken to prevent harm of a patient or to improve the health of a patient—required to be conducted as a result of the vaccine injury qualifies, so long as the vaccine recipient is also hospitalized as an inpatient.
14475: Vaccine Act non-causation issue: redaction of the minor petitioner's name from the published 2012 special master decision under the Vaccine Act and Vaccine Rules. The special master's denial rested on clearly erroneous findings and a legal error about Vaccine Rule 18(b), so the court reversed and remanded for redaction.
the special master's determination was an abuse of discretion.
